CausalChain: Hypoxia in HCC --> Upregulation of HIF-1α --> Increased ENTPD2 expression/activity --> Enhanced conversion of extracellular ATP to AMP --> Recruitment and accumulation of MDSCs in the TME --> Suppression of CTL and NK cell cytotoxicity --> Resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors; Thus, inhibition of ENTPD2 alleviates MDSC accumulation and restores immune function.
Hypothesis: Inhibition of ENTPD2 in hypoxic hepatocellular carcinoma reduces MDSC-mediated immunosuppression and restores effector cell function, thereby enhancing the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors in advanced HCC.
Abstract: Tumor hypoxia in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is well‐documented to drive metabolic alterations that contribute to the establishment of an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Recent studies have highlighted the role of hypoxia‐inducible factor 1α (HIF‐1α) in upregulating enzymes such as ectonucleoside triphosphate diphosphohydrolase 2 (ENTPD2). Increased ENTPD2 activity converts extracellular ATP to 5′ AMP, thereby facilitating the recruitment and accumulation of myeloid‐derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). These MDSCs, in turn, inhibit cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) and natural killer (NK) cell responses by expressing inhibitory ligands, such as PD-L1 and galectin-9, ultimately reducing the efficacies of immunotherapeutic strategies like PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitors. In this review, we propose a novel hypothesis that targets this metabolic axis to overcome immunotherapy resistance in HCC.
